\begin{abstract}
In April 2016 a House of Commons committee heard that new television rules from the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) would cost \lttvJobsTotal{} media jobs by 2020. The figure came from a commissioned study detailed enough to check. I fixed the forecast record and analysis plan before collecting outcomes and compared two of the study's three scenarios with CRTC data for 2016--2019. As planned, specialty and pay channels' revenue, on which most of the job figure depends, was inconsistent with the forecast path at the pre-stated error scale, and distributors' revenue was consistent with it. The study's key input, uptake of an entry-level package, was \lttvUptakeJuneShare{} in mid-2016 against an assumed \lttvByopSixteen{}; a 2017 survey, outside the plan's accepted sources, put it near the study's \lttvByopSeventeen{} for that year. In analyses added after seeing outcomes, the study's chain recalculated at the CRTC's count fits channel revenue but not distributors' losses; at the survey's level it comes closer for distributors but predicts channel losses that didn't occur. The testimony called an economy-wide estimate media jobs, described the study's unreproducible 18\% as a share of current spending, and didn't connect the job figure to the uptake assumption.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} forecast evaluation; ex post analysis; economic impact studies; broadcasting regulation; Canada
